name: Nikhil Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride a cargo e-bike out of a small parcel hub under the railway arches in the city centre. The parcel app loads my route at eight, about sixty drops, mostly offices and flats where vans can't park. Lunchtimes I switch to a food app for an hour. I'm still the slowest on the team at the hub; I spend ages finding the right door in the big blocks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the bike, honestly, and figuring things out. I use an AI app every day, to plan my food hour, to learn a bit of coding in the evenings, even to write my messages to the landlord. Hard is the pay, which is the lowest rate on the hub, and the rent on my room in a shared house. I've got about ten days of money saved, which isn't great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a bit of a letdown, I was ready for something big. I'd still say use the tools, they make the day easier. Nothing wrong with saving time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the hub keeps going and I keep getting faster. Cargo bikes in the city centre aren't going anywhere if nothing radical changes. The problem is just the pay and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and try to move up to the better rate once I'm quicker. I'd keep doing the coding course in the evenings. I'd try to get one month's rent saved by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit itchy, like I want more than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten days of savings is very little. What keeps you from worrying more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hub's busy and they keep hiring, so I don't think I'd lose the job. And I'm only paying for a room. If it went wrong I'd find more food shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you learning in the evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Basic web stuff, with an AI tutor. I'm not great yet. I'd like to get into fixing the software for the hub one day, the scanners and route screens are always crashing.

say: AI turning out small is a **letdown**, but tools still save time.
People should **use the tools**, because they make the working day easier.
think: The **hub keeps going** and I keep getting faster.
My only real problem is the low **pay and rent** on my room.
do: Keep riding and aim for the **better pay rate**.
Continue the evening **coding course** with an AI tutor.
feel: Mostly fine but **itchy** for more than this.
S0.quote: Cargo bikes in the city centre aren't going anywhere if nothing radical changes.
fieldNote: He feels **secure in the job** even with thin savings, because the hub keeps hiring.
Uses **AI daily**, including an evening coding course.
Ambition points to fixing the **hub's software** one day.

steps.text: Keep the cargo bike route from the railway arches hub
Continue evening web coding with an AI tutor
Save one month's room rent by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, get on with it. The ones who learn the tools will be fine. I'd post my AI study setup for anyone who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my bike is safe because robots are slow in the centre. The hub office will shrink, though. Fewer planners, fewer people answering customer calls, and that might be a chance for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the hub manager if I can help set up the new route software, even unpaid at first. I'd keep riding. I'd push my coding course harder, maybe two evenings more a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of worry about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes on booking, planning and customer messages. What changes at the hub?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners in the little office will mostly go. The route will come straight from the system. Somebody has to fix the route system when it sends me to a door that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would more people chasing delivery work hurt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If office people lose jobs, some will come to riding. But most won't want to ride in the rain with sixty parcels, so I'm not too worried.

say: People should **get on with it**; those learning tools will be fine.
I'd share my **AI study setup** online for anyone who wants it.
think: My **bike route** is safe, as robots are slow in the city centre.
A shrinking **hub office** could open a door for me.
do: Ask the hub manager to help set up the **route software**.
Add two more **coding evenings** a week.
feel: **Excited**, with a little worry about rent.
S1.quote: Somebody has to fix the route system when it sends me to a door that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: He sees office cuts at the hub as an **opening**, not a threat.
Willing to work **unpaid at first** to get into the tech side.
Thin savings make him **uneasy**, but his own job looks safe.

steps.text: Volunteer to help set up the hub's new route software
Keep riding the city centre cargo route
Study web coding two extra evenings a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need help fast, but also that sitting still won't save anyone. I'd tell people to learn what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 means my coding course is worthless, because the AI codes better than I ever would. Then robots on the streets around 2031. That's my two plans gone in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride every hour I can and save. I'd try to get a job as someone who watches over delivery robots remotely, because they'll need people at first. I'd move to a cheaper room, or back home to my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ladder I was climbing got pulled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots about three years later. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is when I'd have to jump. The robots will be learning the streets and someone has to sit with them while they do. I'd rather be that someone than the guy they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got ten days of savings. How do you fund a switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By riding more and moving home. My parents have a spare room an hour away. AGI in two years would leave me with a coding course that's worthless and a bike that's next.

say: This is **huge** and people need help fast.
Sitting still **won't save** anyone, so learn what you can.
think: AGI in **2028** makes my coding course worthless.
Robots take the streets around **2031**, ending both my plans.
do: Ride **every hour** available and save the extra.
Apply as a **remote robot supervisor** for delivery firms.
Move to a **cheaper room** or back to his parents.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ladder he was climbing was pulled up.
S2.quote: AGI in two years would leave me with a coding course that's worthless and a bike that's next.
fieldNote: Fast AGI kills **both his plans**: the coding route and the riding.
He aims at the brief window for **robot supervision** work.
Willing to **move home** to cut costs and fund a switch.

steps.text: Ride every available hour and bank the extra
Apply to delivery firms as a remote robot supervisor
Move into his parents' spare room an hour away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people who move now. Don't wait for a scheme to tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes sense of my plan. I'd switch from coding to robot maintenance, the hands-on fixing. Robots arrive around 2034 and they'll need someone to fix them for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the robotics and electrics course at the college in the evenings. I'd use the AI tutor every day. I'd ask the hub if they'd trial me as a technician when the first robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but up for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still go for the coding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the pure coding, no. With AGI coming in 2031, I'd use the AI to code and learn to fix the machines with my hands. That mix is what lasts longest, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your friends at the hub do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most would carry on and hope. My mate Tariq (a rider at the hub) says he'll deal with the robots when they come. I'd try to drag Tariq to the college with me.

say: **Five years** is enough for people who move now.
People shouldn't **wait for a scheme** to tell them what to do.
think: I'd switch from coding to **robot maintenance**, the hands-on fixing.
Robots arrive around **2034** and will need fixers for years.
do: Take the **robotics and electrics** course at college in the evenings.
Ask the hub to trial him as a **technician**.
S3.quote: My mate Tariq (a rider at the hub) says he'll deal with the robots when they come.
fieldNote: He reshapes his plan around the **thinking-first, robots-later** sequence.
Combines **AI for coding** with hands-on repair skills.
Still expects to lose **riding income**, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Take the evening robotics and electrics course at the college
Study with the AI tutor every day
Ask the hub to trial him as a robot technician

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is great news, if people use it. I'd tell everyone at the hub to start something now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I've got time to get properly good, not just good enough. I'd still be young when the robots come in 2039. My worry is more about rent this year than about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course over two years and keep riding. Then I'd try for a technician job at a robot firm. I'd keep using AI tools for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. How does your plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a year to save properly first. Ten days of money is not a base for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small repair team for the delivery robots, maybe the same hub under the arches. That would be a nice full circle.

say: **Ten years** is great news for riders, if people actually use it.
Everyone at the hub should **start something** now.
think: I have time to become **properly good**, not just good enough.
My bigger worry is **this year's rent**, not 2036.
do: Do the **robotics course** over two years while riding.
Apply for **technician jobs** at robot firms.
S4.quote: Ten days of money is not a base for anything.
fieldNote: Ten years makes his **ambition** realistic rather than a rushed gamble.
Recognises his **thin savings** must come first.
Imagines leading a **repair team** at the same hub.

steps.text: Save properly for a year before studying
Complete a two-year robotics course while riding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be halfway up a ladder that disappears. What would help is cheap evening courses in robotics and a deal where robot firms hire people from the jobs they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I'm scared. Not really, of the robots. I'm scared of being 30 and still on ten days of savings, whatever the robots do.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of being 30 and still on ten days of savings, whatever the robots do.
portrait: Nikhil is **27**, rides a cargo e-bike from a city centre parcel hub and rents a room.
He uses **AI daily**, studies coding in the evenings and wants into the tech side.
Fast AGI wipes out **both his plans**, so he'd aim for robot supervision and move home.
With more time he'd retrain in **robot repair**, though his thin savings come first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the ladder he's climbing would vanish.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **robotics courses** and robot firms **hiring** from replaced jobs.
